title: Oncology problems as QUBOs
summary: Biomarker-panel selection, radiotherapy planning, docking and folding written as binary optimisation; what annealers and QAOA have actually achieved; then a gene-panel lab that checks whether the optimum generalises.

shots.title:
Oncology problems
as QUBOs.
shots.subtitle: Panels, beams, poses — and the classical solver next door.
shots.narration: Many oncology problems are choices among many discrete options: which genes in a panel, which beam intensities, which docking pose. Written as binary optimisation, they become inputs for annealers and QAOA.

notes: the input format for annealers and QAOA
shots.narration: The common format is the QUBO: minimise x transpose Q x over binary vectors. Constraints become penalty terms, such as lambda times the squared difference between the number chosen and k.

shots.text: Solvers: **QAOA** (with constraint-preserving mixers), **quantum annealing** — and the classical baseline, **simulated annealing**.
shots.narration: Three solvers matter here. QAOA alternates cost and mixing steps, and a constraint-preserving mixer keeps it inside valid solutions. Quantum annealing steers hardware toward low energies. And classical simulated annealing is the baseline to beat.

notes: r_i: relevance of gene i to the outcome
R_ij: redundancy between genes i and j
shots.narration: Biomarker panels first. Choose k genes that are individually relevant to the outcome but not redundant with each other. That is the classic max-relevance, min-redundancy criterion, and it writes naturally as a QUBO.

shots.label: possible panels from just 20 candidate genes (2²⁰)
shots.context: and 20,000 genes is the real search space
shots.narration: The search space explodes: twenty candidate genes already give over a million possible panels. That growth is the only reason to want a better optimiser.

shots.text: First quantum-annealing radiotherapy test (2015): annealing was **3–4× faster** but reached **worse plans** than simulated annealing.
shots.narration: Radiotherapy planning was tried on an annealer in 2015, on two prostate cases with reduced beamlets. The annealer ran three to four times faster than the classical methods — but reached worse plans than simulated annealing on both patients.

shots.text: **Docking** maps to finding a **maximum-weight clique**; Gaussian boson samplers can be programmed to sample such cliques.
shots.narration: Docking can be cast as finding a maximum-weight clique in a graph of possible contacts, and Gaussian boson samplers can be programmed to sample such cliques — shown for a ligand binding a target linked to immune disease and cancer.

shots.text: Lattice **protein folding**: on an annealer with up to **81** qubits (2012); a 10-residue peptide on **22** qubits in simulation (2021).
shots.narration: Coarse-grained protein folding has been run on an annealer with up to eighty-one qubits in 2012, and with a variational algorithm, a ten-residue peptide on twenty-two simulated qubits in 2021. Real proteins are far larger.

shots.text: In every case, ask one thing first: what did the **best classical solver** get, on the same problem, with the same budget?
shots.narration: In every case, ask one question first: what did the best classical solver get, on the same problem, with the same time budget? The radiotherapy study is honest about it; many papers are not.

shots.text: In 2026 a Q4Bio team took **quantum feature selection** for cancer biomarkers to real hardware — its claimed gain is **not yet peer-reviewed**.
shots.narration: This is live research. A Wellcome Leap team took quantum feature selection for cancer biomarkers, forecasting treatment response in head-and-neck cancer, onto real hardware. Its claimed improvement over classical methods is not yet peer-reviewed.

shots.text: Lab: build the panel QUBO, solve it three ways — then check whether the optimum **generalises**.
shots.narration: In the lab, you'll build the panel QUBO on synthetic data, solve it by brute force, annealing and QAOA, and then ask the question that matters: does the optimal panel actually predict better in new patients?

steps.title: Lab: a biomarker panel as a QUBO
steps.brief: Synthetic data. Look at the genes first, then solve for k = 2 and 3 with α = 0, 0.5 and 1.5, and compare validation accuracy each time.

steps.title: Notebook: gene panel
steps.brief: Save your best comparison, then interpret it.

fields.label: What happened to validation accuracy at α = 0, 0.5 and 1.5? Explain why too little and too much redundancy penalty both hurt.
Did the solver (brute force, annealing, QAOA) change the panel's accuracy? What, then, could a quantum solver ever contribute here?

questions.prompt: How many distinct panels of exactly 3 genes can be chosen from 8?
questions.explain: 8!/(3!·5!) = 56 — the number of states QAOA's constraint-preserving mixer explores in the lab.

questions.prompt: Selecting a panel from 500 candidate genes with one binary variable per gene: how many qubits does a direct QUBO encoding need?
questions.explain: One variable per gene, one qubit per variable — before any embedding overhead on hardware with limited connectivity.

questions.prompt: In the first quantum-annealing radiotherapy study, how did annealing compare with simulated annealing?
questions.explain: Objective 16.9 v. 6.7 and 70.7 v. 22.9 (lower is better), in 27–38% of the time.

questions.prompt: What does the penalty λ(Σx − k)² do if λ is set too small?
options: The optimum may choose the wrong number of genes
questions.explain: Too weak a penalty lets the objective trade feasibility for score — the classic QUBO tuning problem.

fields.label: 1. Variables, objective and constraints as a QUBO. Count the binary variables.
2. How would you choose the penalty weights, and how would you check the solver's answer is feasible?
3. Name at least two classical baselines (e.g. simulated annealing, integer programming) and the comparison you would run.
